nameStory: Rose blackberry gets its name from being part of the rose family, sharing the characteristic thorny stems and five-petaled flowers with garden roses. The 'blackberry' part comes from its dark purple-black fruits that ripen in late summer, though like many brambles, the berries actually start red before turning their final dark color.
description: Rose blackberry is a thorny shrub that grows 3-6 feet tall, forming dense thickets through underground stems. It's one of New England's native highbush blackberries, with arching canes covered in sharp prickles. The plant produces clusters of white five-petaled flowers in late spring, followed by edible dark berries in summer. Like other brambles, it has compound leaves typically divided into three to five leaflets.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white flowers with five rounded petals appear in small clusters, each flower about an inch across with a sweet, mild fragrance and numerous yellow stamens in the center

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 3-5 oval leaflets that have serrated edges and feel slightly rough on top, smooth underneath, with the terminal leaflet noticeably larger than the side ones

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Aggregate berries start red and ripen to deep purple-black, composed of many small drupelets clustered together, sweet-tart when fully ripe and easily pulled from the white core

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, arching canes armed with curved prickles that feel sharp to the touch, turning from green to reddish-brown as they mature, with a waxy coating that can be rubbed off

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies through underground runners, with biennial canes that grow vegetatively the first year and flower and fruit the second year before dying back

habitat: Rose blackberry thrives in forest edges, clearings, and partially shaded areas with well-drained soil. You'll often find it along woodland borders, in old fields returning to forest, and beside trails where it gets some sunlight but isn't in full sun all day. It prefers slightly acidic soil and can tolerate both moist and drier conditions.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in early spring, followed by clusters of fragrant white flowers in late May to early June that attract bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Berries ripen from red to dark purple-black from July through August, while new green canes grow vigorously with fresh leaves.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to reddish before dropping, revealing the thorny canes, while fruiting canes begin to die back after completing their two-year cycle.
seasonality.winter: Bare thorny canes are visible, with living canes showing reddish-brown bark and small buds, while old fruiting canes appear gray and brittle.

funFact: Rose blackberry canes live exactly two years in a precise schedule: they spend their entire first year just growing leaves and storing energy, then in their second year they flower, fruit, and die - meaning every berry you eat comes from a cane that's in its final season of life.
confusionNotes: Rose blackberry is easily confused with other native blackberries like Allegheny blackberry, but rose blackberry tends to prefer slightly more shaded conditions and has leaflets that feel distinctly rougher on top. Remember: if it's growing in deep shade rather than full sun, it's more likely to be rose blackberry.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'blackberry' can be confusing because many species in the Rubus genus are called blackberries, and they readily hybridize with each other. What most people call 'wild blackberries' are actually several different species that are very difficult to tell apart without close examination.
compareHints: Rose blackberry differs from red raspberry by having darker fruit that doesn't separate from the white core when picked. Unlike dewberries, it grows upright rather than trailing along the ground. Compared to other upright blackberries, rose blackberry tolerates more shade and has distinctly rougher-textured leaflet surfaces.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple-flowered raspberry stands out from all other New England brambles because it's completely thornless and has those distinctive large magenta flowers.

Among New England's brambles, black raspberry is unique for its waxy blue-coated canes - red raspberries have brown or reddish canes without the coating, while blackberries have green to brown canes that are often more angular.

Among its bramble relatives, wineberry stands out with its distinctively fuzzy, reddish stems that look almost velvety compared to the smoother canes of black raspberry or the more prominently thorny stems of blackberries.
Unlike every other bramble in New England, dewdrop has no thorns and produces dry fruits instead of juicy berries.
Among New England brambles, red raspberry is unique for its red, hollow-cored fruits.
Swamp dewberry stands out from other New England brambles by its preference for wet habitats and ground-hugging growth habit.
Unlike all other Rubus species in New England, dwarf raspberry stays completely low to the ground and lacks any thorns or prickles.
Allegheny blackberry is the most robust and widespread of New England's blackberries, with larger thorns and taller growth than most dewberries, which tend to trail along the ground.
Among New England's many Rubus species, common dewberry is distinguished by its strongly trailing habit—while swamp dewberry also grows low, it's less robust and prefers wetter areas.

Cloudberry stands out dramatically from all other New England brambles by its tiny, ground-hugging stature and lack of thorny canes - while red raspberries, blackberries, and dewberries all form arching or trailing woody stems.
Among all the brambles in New England, cutleaf blackberry stands out dramatically with its deeply divided, lacy leaves - no other Rubus species has anything close to this leaf shape.

Among New England's many Rubus species, smooth blackberry stands out for its nearly thornless stems - most relatives like Allegheny blackberry and black raspberry are heavily armed with thorns or prickles.
Sand blackberry differs from its common relatives by its consistently low growth habit and distinctive wedge-shaped leaflets.
Among New England's many Rubus species, Armenian Blackberry stands out for its exceptional vigor and large fruit size.
Among the many New England blackberries, Old Field Blackberry is distinguished by its preference for disturbed, sunny habitats rather than forest settings.

Among New England's many brambles, bristly blackberry stands out for its uniformly dense, fine bristles rather than scattered large thorns like Allegheny blackberry, or the smooth stems of smooth blackberry.
Unlike our native dewberries which have green to reddish canes, European dewberry's blue-white waxy coating is unmistakable.

Within the bramble family, Green Mountain Blackberry differs from red raspberries by its darker fruit and more aggressive bristles, and from dewberries by its upright rather than trailing growth habit.
Pennsylvania Blackberry differs from black raspberries by having solid white pith in the canes (raspberries have hollow stems) and berries that don't separate from their white core when picked.
Small-leaf bramble stands out from native New England brambles primarily by its much smaller leaflets and colored flowers.
Unlike the more common Allegheny blackberry or red raspberry found throughout New England, Rubus multispinus has significantly more spines per stem segment.
Pugnacious blackberry differs from red and black raspberries by having solid stems (raspberries are hollow) and berries that don't separate from their white core when picked.
Unlike its bramble relatives with their thorny canes, compound leaves, and juicy berries, robin runaway has no thorns, simple heart-shaped leaves, and dry fuzzy fruits.
Rubus flavinanus is believed to be intermediate between Allegheny blackberry (which is common and forms large colonies) and Bristly blackberry (which has notably bristly stems).
Unlike the upright Allegheny blackberry or arching black raspberry, northeastern dewberry stays close to the ground with its trailing habit.
Among New England's many blackberries, Yankee Blackberry is part of the 'true blackberry' group with upright to arching canes, as opposed to dewberries which trail along the ground.
Unlike upright blackberries like Allegheny Blackberry that form tall arching canes, Ecotone Blackberry stays low and trailing like other dewberries.
Among New England's many Rubus species, upland dewberry is distinguished by its preference for dry, upland sites combined with its trailing growth habit.
Among New England's many brambles, this species falls in the middle range for thorniness - more prickly than smooth blackberry but less aggressive than bristly blackberry.
Smith's blackberry differs from the more common Allegheny blackberry in subtle details of leaf shape and flower structure, though these differences require close examination.
Among New England's many Rubus species, thicket dewberry is distinguished by being the most committed to staying flat against the ground.
Unlike the common Allegheny Blackberry with its sturdy thorns or the smooth-stemmed Red Raspberry, Bicknell's Bristleberry has that distinctive bristly texture without true thorns.
